name: Rodriguez v. County of Los Angeles
court: Ninth Circuit (from the Central District of California)
topic: Eighth Amendment excessive force during jail cell extractions; beatings and Taser use on non-resisting and unconscious prisoners; qualified immunity after a jury verdict; supervisory liability for sergeants, a lieutenant, and a captain; Monell custom of condoning force; the Bane Act
summary: After a disturbance in two high security units of the Los Angeles County Men's Central Jail in 2008, extraction teams entered cells and, on the evidence the jury accepted, beat, stomped, and repeatedly Tasered prisoners who were not resisting, some after they were handcuffed and some after they were unconscious. A jury found nineteen sheriff's department employees and the County liable and awarded $740,000 in compensatory and $210,000 in punitive damages. The Ninth Circuit affirmed everything, holding that the law clearly prohibited malicious and sadistic force in quelling a disturbance, that the sergeants who directed the teams and the lieutenant and captain who watched were liable as supervisors, and that the jury could infer a County custom of condoning force from the department's failure to investigate and discipline.
coverage: The opinion was read in full, including the staff summary and all sections on jurisdiction, exhaustion, immunity, the Bane Act, Monell, juror bias, punitive damages, trial errors, and attorney's fees, from the Ninth Circuit's opinion datastore at https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2018/05/30/13-56292.pdf.

The docket numbers 13-56292 and 14-55374, the filing date of May 30, 2018, and the panel (W. Fletcher and Ikuta, Circuit Judges, and Barker, District Judge, sitting by designation; W. Fletcher writing) were confirmed from that file. The slip opinion's running head styles the case Rodriguez v. Cruz; the County of Los Angeles is a named defendant. The slip opinion does not print the Federal Reporter citation; 891 F.3d 776 is the citation as assigned for this brief and was not confirmed from the source read.

The facts are the facts as the Ninth Circuit related them in the light most favorable to the prevailing plaintiffs, drawn largely from the plaintiffs' trial testimony. The trial record, the Citizens' Commission on Jail Violence report, and the district court's rulings were not read.

The opinion also resolves procedural issues (Chuman certification, PLRA exhaustion, juror bias, deposition testimony, attorney's fees of $5,378,174.66 with a 2.0 multiplier). Those holdings are noted but not developed for training purposes.
facts:
The facts are related, as the Ninth Circuit related them, in the light most favorable to the prisoners who won at trial (slip op. at 9).

On August 25, 2008, prisoners in two high security, single cell units of the Los Angeles County Men's Central Jail lit fires, flooded toilets, shattered sinks, and threw shards of porcelain. Captain Daniel Cruz, the unit commander, and Lieutenant Christopher Blasnek, the incident commander, planned cell extractions. Prisoners would be given a chance to cuff up and leave voluntarily; those who refused would be extracted by sergeant-led teams, with shield deputies entering first to pin or knock down the prisoner, capture deputies to restrain him, and Taser deputies to apply shocks in stun mode if he could not be subdued. Policy required the lowest possible level of force to overcome only the resistance confronting the team and prohibited force as punishment (at 9-10).

Five prisoners testified. Masked deputies fired a 40 mm block gun into Carlos Flores's cell, threw concussion grenades, pushed him down with a shield, and five or six deputies punched and kicked his face, head, and body while alternating Taser applications and yelling "stop resisting" as he said he was not. His nose and eye socket were broken; he woke in a hospital, where surgeons placed plates and screws to rebuild the socket (at 10-11). Juan Carlos Sanchez was handcuffed, then punched, kicked, and stomped until his ankle broke, dragged out unconscious, and Tasered again outside the cell (at 11-12). Erik Nunez was shot with block gun rounds, kicked, beaten, and Tasered repeatedly, including between his buttocks by a laughing deputy (at 12-13). Juan Trinidad's hand was broken by a block gun round before entry; five deputies then beat and Tasered him, twisting the broken hand, and continued after he was handcuffed. His back was broken in several places (at 13-14). Heriberto Rodriguez, a pretrial detainee, had his arm twisted until the elbow bent the wrong way and was beaten and Tasered after handcuffing, including in the groin area (at 14).

Policy required extractions to be videotaped in full and the tapes preserved. The forty-one tapes produced showed almost nothing inside the cells and, per the plaintiffs' expert, not one of the hundred plus hard strikes the deputies' own reports described. At least five tapes likely to show the beatings were never produced (at 15-16). The plaintiffs also offered a county commission report finding that senior management failed to investigate excessive force, a former supervisor's testimony that force incidents rose sharply under Cruz and that he condoned excessive force by investigating improperly or not at all, and evidence that dozens of incidents, including these, were missing from the force tracking system (at 20).

After a month long trial the jury found against nineteen employees and the County, awarding $740,000 in compensatory damages and $210,000 in punitive damages against the five supervisors (at 21).
holding:
Affirmed in full. Judge W. Fletcher wrote for the panel.

Sufficiency and the Eighth Amendment. The jury was instructed that it had to find excessive and unnecessary force, that the defendants acted maliciously and sadistically for the purpose of causing harm, and causation. The defendants argued the force was justified by resistance. The court called the argument meritless: there was "abundant evidence presented to the jury that appellants inflicted severe injuries on appellees while they were not resisting, and even while they were unconscious," and the jury could reasonably find the force was not a good faith effort to maintain or restore discipline (slip op. at 31). Rodriguez, a pretrial detainee, should have had the objective Kingsley standard; the error was forfeited and harmless because he prevailed under the harder one (at 16-17).

Clearly established law for the deputies. Hudson's good faith standard "sets forth the clearly established law" for force used in quelling a prison disturbance, and cases decided well before 2008 gave notice. "[N]o reasonable officer in appellants' positions would have believed that beating a prisoner to the point of serious injury, unconsciousness, or hospitalization solely to cause him pain was constitutionally permissible" (at 32-33).

Tasers. The Taser deputies argued the law on Tasers was unclear in 2008, relying on the Fourth Amendment decisions in Bryan v. MacPherson and Mattos v. Agarano. The court disagreed. An officer "is not entitled to qualified immunity on the grounds that the law is not clearly established every time a novel method is used to inflict injury," and the circuit had said in 1988 that a Taser is a painful and dangerous device not to be used unnecessarily or solely to punish or inflict pain. The Fourth Amendment asks objective reasonableness while the Eighth turns on intent; once a jury finds malicious and sadistic use of more than de minimis force, the Eighth Amendment "always" is violated (at 33-36).

Supervisors. A supervisor is liable for personal involvement or a sufficient causal connection, including "setting in motion a series of acts by others or by knowingly refus[ing] to terminate a series of acts by others" the supervisor knew or reasonably should have known would cause constitutional injury, and for culpable action or inaction in training, supervision, or control, acquiescence, or reckless or callous indifference (at 37). The sergeants conceded they were present and directed the force; that sufficed. The disturbance did not by itself justify their inaction, because Whitley long ago established that malicious and sadistic force violates the Eighth Amendment even in quelling a disturbance posing significant risks (at 37-38). Cruz and Blasnek, to the extent they observed and knowingly refused to terminate the deputies' acts, were liable for the same reasons; ample evidence showed they directed and observed most extractions. Even assuming Cruz did not watch two of them, the jury could find he knowingly maintained a culture of impunity and disabled the procedures for identifying excessive force, which was culpable inaction in training, supervision, or control (at 38-39).

Monell. Deliberate indifference may be shown by a failure to investigate and discipline in the face of widespread violations, and a custom can be inferred from repeated violations without discipline. The commission report, the former supervisor's testimony, the missing tracking entries, and evidence that supervisors watched and did nothing were substantial evidence of a custom of condoning excessive force that proximately caused the beatings (at 46-48).

Other holdings. The Chuman, exhaustion, Bane Act, juror bias, punitive damages, evidentiary, instruction, and fee challenges all failed (at 21-29, 39-46, 49-60).
notDecided:
Whether the deputies' account was true. The appeal followed a jury verdict, so the court related and accepted the prisoners' version of events. It did not independently find that any particular deputy struck any particular blow; it held that the evidence permitted the jury's findings (slip op. at 9, 31).

Whether cell extraction tactics as planned were unconstitutional. The court's holdings concern force used on prisoners who were not resisting or were unconscious, not the use of shield, capture, and Taser teams as such, or the use of block guns and grenades to open a cell (at 9-10).

The Fourteenth Amendment standard for Rodriguez. The court noted that the pretrial detainee should have been judged under Kingsley's objective standard, but treated the issue as forfeited and harmless (at 16-17).

Whether Captain Cruz personally observed the Nunez and Rodriguez extractions. The court assumed he did not and found liability on the causal connection theory instead (at 38-39).

The content of any required training. The Monell holding rested on a custom of failing to investigate and discipline, not on a specific training deficiency (at 47-48).
inPractice:
The holding that reaches every jail deputy is that the Eighth Amendment line was clearly established long before 2008: more than minimal force used maliciously and sadistically to cause harm, rather than in a good faith effort to restore order, violates the Constitution, and a riot does not change that. Force on a prisoner who has stopped resisting, is handcuffed, or is unconscious is the fact pattern the court kept returning to.

The "stop resisting" refrain was evidence against the deputies, not for them. Each prisoner testified that deputies shouted it while he was not resisting, and the audio captured the words without video of the prisoner. Commands are not a substitute for a record of actual resistance. The missing tapes mattered too: policy required recording the whole extraction, the tapes produced showed none of the strikes the deputies' own reports described, and the court upheld an instruction that the defendants violated their own preservation policy.

The Taser holding warns against reading Fourth Amendment cases into custody. The deputies argued Bryan and Mattos showed Taser law was unsettled. The court said those were objective reasonableness cases; in the Eighth Amendment setting the question is intent, and a jury finding of malicious and sadistic use settles it.

For supervisors, presence plus direction was enough. The sergeants who ran the teams conceded they were there and directed the force. The lieutenant and captain who observed and did not stop it were liable for knowingly refusing to terminate it. The captain was also liable for the culture: investigating badly or not at all, and letting force go untracked. Punitive damages were assessed only against the five supervisors.
trainIt:
Dr. Sowards teaches Rodriguez in the custody standards line with Kingsley, Whitley v. Albers, Hudson v. McMillian, and Pierce v. Multnomah County, as the case that shows what the Whitley and Hudson standard looks like when a jury applies it to a planned operation that came apart inside the cells.

Train cell extraction as a sequence with a hard stop. The plan here was lawful on paper: an order to cuff up, a shield entry, a capture team, a Taser only if the prisoner could not be subdued, the lowest level of force needed, and no force as punishment. Train the point at which the prisoner is controlled or cuffed and every further strike or Taser cycle must be justified by new resistance.

Train the record. Force is recorded in full because policy says so and because the tape is the defense when resistance was real. A report describing hard strikes, with a tape that shows none, is the record this jury saw. "Stop resisting" is a command for when a person is resisting, not a narration.

Train supervisors to the court's standard. A sergeant who directs the team owns the force. A lieutenant or captain who watches and does not stop unlawful force owns it. A captain who fails to investigate, discipline, and track force can be liable for the next incident even if he was not in the room, and the agency can be liable for the custom.

Teach the standards side by side, and teach that force which is malicious and sadistic fails every one of them.

Teach the posture. This was a jury verdict, affirmed. The facts are the prisoners' testimony as the jury accepted it, not findings the court made on its own.

The facts are the prisoners' testimony as the court related it in the light most favorable to the verdict; the deputies disputed them at trial. The Bane Act, exhaustion, juror bias, and fee holdings are summarized only.

applications.title: A riot does not suspend the Eighth Amendment
applications.body: The court held that Whitley long ago established that malicious and sadistic force violates the Eighth Amendment even while quelling a disturbance that poses significant risks. Force on a prisoner who is not resisting, is handcuffed, or is unconscious was the conduct the jury punished.

applications.title: "Stop resisting" is a command, not a narration
applications.body: Every prisoner testified that deputies shouted it while he was not resisting, and the audio captured the words without video of the prisoner. Give the command when there is resistance, and make sure the record shows the resistance.

applications.title: Record all of it and keep all of it
applications.body: Policy required taping entire extractions. The tapes produced showed none of the hundred plus hard strikes in the deputies' own reports, and at least five tapes were never produced. The jury was told the defendants violated their own preservation policy.

applications.title: Street Taser law does not rescue a custody beating
applications.body: The deputies argued Bryan and Mattos left Taser law unsettled in 2008. The court said those are Fourth Amendment cases; in custody the question is intent, and a 1988 decision already said Tasers may not be used unnecessarily or to inflict pain.

applications.title: Supervisors who direct or watch are liable
applications.body: The sergeants who ran the teams, and the lieutenant and captain who observed and did not stop the force, were held individually liable. Punitive damages were assessed only against the five supervisors. The captain was also liable for a culture of impunity built on failing to investigate and track force.

quiz.q: What standard did the court apply to the convicted prisoners' excessive force claims arising from the cell extractions?
options: Eighth Amendment: whether force was applied in a good faith effort to maintain or restore discipline or maliciously and sadistically to cause harm
Strict liability for any injury during an extraction
quiz.teach: The jury was instructed on the Hudson and Whitley standard and found malicious and sadistic intent. The court said that standard was clearly established for force used in quelling a prison disturbance long before 2008.

quiz.q: Why did the court reject the Taser deputies' argument that Bryan v. MacPherson and Mattos v. Agarano showed the law on Tasers was unsettled in 2008?
options: Because those cases were decided by other circuits
Because those are Fourth Amendment objective reasonableness cases, while the Eighth Amendment turns on intent, and a jury finding of malicious and sadistic use settles the violation
Because the deputies used stun mode rather than dart mode
quiz.teach: The court explained the different standards and added that the circuit had said in 1988 that Tasers are painful and dangerous devices not to be used unnecessarily or solely to punish or inflict pain.

quiz.q: On what basis did the court hold Captain Cruz liable even assuming he did not personally watch two of the extractions?
options: Respondeat superior, because he commanded the unit

A sufficient causal connection: the jury could find he knowingly created and maintained a culture of impunity and disabled the procedures for identifying excessive force, which was culpable inaction in training, supervision, or control
He was not held liable for those two extractions
He personally ordered the Taser use
quiz.teach: The court applied the supervisory liability framework of Starr v. Baca: personal involvement or a sufficient causal connection, including setting in motion or knowingly refusing to terminate a series of acts and culpable inaction in supervision and control.
